facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
The applicants in the Chrysostomos and Papachrysostomou v. Turkey case also took part in the demonstration of 19 July 1989 in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
The applicant in the Loizidou v. Turkey case also took part in the demonstration of 19 July 1989 in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held on the fifteenth anniversary of the Turkish intervention in Cyprus.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held in support of the missing persons and to protest against human rights violations.
The applicant joined the demonstration of 19 July 1989 as a reporter for the newspaper Exormisis.
During the demonstration of 19 July 1989, dozens of armed Turkish policemen and soldiers moved towards the demonstrators.
During the demonstration of 19 July 1989, the UN peacekeeping cordon broke up and vanished.
During the demonstration of 19 July 1989, Turkish forces started to beat some women demonstrators with batons, to kick them and drag them by the arms, legs and hair.
While the applicant was trying to help some of the women demonstrators, he was grabbed and beaten by Turkish policemen.
The applicant was hit in the face and other parts of the body by Turkish policemen during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant was taken at gunpoint together with others who had also been arrested during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant's photographic equipment was seized despite him showing his press card during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant was led to a bus through an angry crowd of 200-300 civilians who shouted abuse and threats at him.
As the applicant was walking without police protection, the crowd had an opportunity to rush at him, and he was dragged and beaten until two policemen came and accompanied him onto the bus.
The applicant was transported to the so-called "Pavlides Garage", where a body search was carried out and all his personal effects were taken.
At the so-called "Pavlides Garage", the crowd outside was shouting and throwing stones, some of which came through the roof.
While at the so-called "Pavlides Garage", the applicant saw a policeman in civilian clothes who told him "Turkey will kill you".
Sometime around midnight at the so-called "Pavlides Garage", the applicant was interrogated by an officer who spoke perfect Greek.
The applicant did not give wholly accurate answers to some of the questions during the interrogation, preferring to lie about some of the detail.
The interrogating officer started a political discussion and tried to convey his own ideas to the applicant in a very friendly and diplomatic manner.
The applicant refused to sign a statement written in Turkish, as he considered it would have been tantamount to recognising the "Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus" (the "TRNC").
When one of the women detainees (Mrs Vrahimi, application no. 16078/90) was beaten at the so-called "Pavlides Garage", all the other prisoners remained silent, fearing for their fate.
At around 2.30 a.m. on 20 July 1989, the applicant and some other men were ordered onto a police bus.
The applicant was taken to the Seray Police Station, where, after a body search, he was held in a cell that was filthy, dirty and dark.
During his stay in the cell at the Seray Police Station, the applicant heard the screams of other demonstrators.
At around 2.00 p.m. on 20 July 1989, the applicant was given back his personal effects and taken to court together with seven other prisoners.
No proper translation was provided at the court hearing on 20 July 1989.
At the court hearing on 20 July 1989, a policeman acted as translator but translated only part of what the judge and the witnesses said.
At the court hearing on 20 July 1989, the accused explained why they were taking part in the demonstration and in what capacity.
The applicant was remanded in custody for two days following the court hearing on 20 July 1989.
The applicant was taken to Ortakeuy Prison, where all his personal effects were removed again.
At Ortakeuy Prison, the applicant was put with other men in a dormitory block.
An hour after being placed in the dormitory block at Ortakeuy Prison, the applicant was blindfolded and led to another area of the prison.
At Ortakeuy Prison, the applicant was interrogated by four or five army officers who could not speak any Greek, with a translator present.
The interrogation at Ortakeuy Prison touched on political and military subjects.
After the interrogation at Ortakeuy Prison, the applicant was taken to another room to talk to a television anchorman.
On 21 July 1989, the applicant was again taken to court together with nine other people.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the applicant had no legal representation.

At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, no proper interpretation was provided, and the interpreter had difficulties in translating some of the words and was occasionally helped by the television anchorman.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, one of the accused (the Bishop of Kitium) spoke on behalf of the others and said they would only accept as defence counsel a Greek-Cypriot or a UN lawyer.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the trial judge replied that she could only appoint a lawyer registered with the "TRNC" bar association.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the accused pleaded "not guilty" and stated that they did not recognise the legitimacy of the "TRNC" and of its tribunals.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, four witnesses were called by the prosecution.

At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the Bishop of Kitium put some questions to the first prosecution witness, but those considered of a political character were ruled inadmissible by the trial judge.

At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the Bishop of Kitium made the following statement: "since cross-examining the pseudo-witnesses of your pseudo-court may be regarded as indicating that we recognise the procedure, we say that we have nothing else to say and we shall not cross-examine any other pseudo-witness".
From the point of the Bishop of Kitium's statement at the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the accused did not participate in the procedure.
After the trial hearing on 21 July 1989, the applicant and his co-accused were taken back to prison and their pictures were taken.
On 22 July 1989, the applicant was taken to court again.
On 22 July 1989, a baying crowd gathered outside the courtroom.
On 22 July 1989, the applicant was sentenced to three days' imprisonment and a fine of 50 Cypriot pounds (CYP) – approximately 85 euros (EUR).
The sentence imposed on the applicant on 22 July 1989 included five additional days in prison in default of payment of the fine within 24 hours.
On 22 July 1989, there was an angry crowd in the court area shouting, swearing and making obscene gestures at the applicant and the other detainees.
The applicant was detained in Ortakeuy Prison from 24 until 28 July 1989.

During his detention in Ortakeuy Prison from 24 until 28 July 1989, the applicant refused to eat anything in order to protest against the prison director's refusal to give to the Bishop of Kitium the church vestments and holy vessels, which had been sent in order to allow the Bishop to celebrate mass.
On 26 July 1989, the applicant was locked in an isolation cell at Ortakeuy Prison as punishment for refusing food.
The isolation cell at Ortakeuy Prison in which the applicant was placed on 26 July 1989 was extremely small and unbearably hot (40-60°C).
On 28 July 1989, the applicant was released in front of journalists and television cameras.
On 28 July 1989, the applicant was handed over to UN soldiers at the last Turkish sentry box and transported back to the southern part of Cyprus.
In support of his claim of ill-treatment, the applicant produced five medical certificates.

A certificate issued on 16 December 2002 by Dr. Andreas G. Constantinides, consultant surgeon at the Evangelistria Medical Centre in Nicosia, stated that Mr Tasos Asproftas (the applicant) is suffering from osteoarthritis of the cervical cord and that Dr. Constantinides recommended he stay at home and undergo physiotherapy from 17 December until 28 December 2002.

A certificate issued on an unspecified date by Dr. S.C. Sergiou, orthopaedic surgeon in Larnaka, stated that Mr Tasos Asproftas (the applicant) is suffering from cervical disc disease and is unable to work from 3 January 2003 until 12 January 2003.

A certificate issued on 9 January 2003 by the medical and public health services – X-rays department – of the Republic of Cyprus stated that Mr Tasos Asproftas (the applicant) had a rear central hernia of the disc, rear lateral right osteophyte in the area of chronic hernia of the disc A4-A5, rear lateral left osteophyte in the area of chronic hernia in discs A5-A6 and A6-A7, straight cervical spine due to muscles' spasm, and stenosis of the middle sections of the spinal cord A4-A5 and A5-A6.

A certificate issued on an unspecified date by Dr. Nicos Chr. Spanos, neurosurgeon in Nicosia, recommended that Mr Asproftas (the applicant) be granted sick leave from 13 January 2003 until 31 January 2003 for investigation and treatment of the cervical middle spinal disc.

A certificate issued on 7 February 2003 by Dr. Nicolas C. Christodoulou, specialist in physical medicine and rehabilitation sport medicine in Limassol, diagnosed Mr Asproftas (the applicant) with severe left cervicobranchial syndrome (radiculitis C7) and instructed approximately 12 sessions of physiotherapy including interferential current, short wave diathermy, and mild cervical massage.

The applicant alleged that his health problems (osteoarthritis of the cervical cord, cervical disc disease, and related conditions) were the result of the savage blows he had received from Turkish policemen, soldiers and civilians in July 1989.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators, supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration, were demanding that the "Green Line" in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the "TRNC".
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.
The Government alleged that no force was used against demonstrators who did not intrude into the "TRNC" border area.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.
The Government alleged that no one was ill-treated during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The Government alleged that it was possible that some of the demonstrators had hurt themselves in the confusion or in attempting to scale barbed wire or other fencing.

The Government alleged that had the Turkish police, or anyone else, assaulted or beaten any of the demonstrators, the UN Secretary General would no doubt have referred to this in his report to the Security Council.
The Government alleged that the applicant was charged, tried, found guilty and sentenced to a short term of imprisonment.
The Government alleged that the applicant pleaded not guilty but did not give evidence and declined to use the available judicial remedies.
The Government alleged that the applicant was asked if he required assistance from a lawyer registered in the "TRNC", but refused and did not ask for legal representation.
The Government alleged that interpretation services were provided at the trial by qualified interpreters and that all the proceedings were translated into Greek.

In his report of 7 December 1989 on the UN operations in Cyprus, the UN Secretary General stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.
In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by UNFICYP and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that a short while later, Turkish-Cypriot police and security forces elements forced their way into the area and apprehended 111 persons, 101 of them women.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the Ayios Kassianos school complex is situated in the UN buffer zone, but that the Turkish forces claim it to be on their side of the cease-fire line.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that under working arrangements with UNFICYP, the Turkish-Cypriot security forces had patrolled the Ayios Kassianos school grounds for several years within specific restrictions, and that this patrolling ceased altogether as part of the unmanning agreement implemented in May 1989.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that in the afternoon of 21 July 1989, some 300 Greek Cypriots gathered at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia to protest the continuing detention by the Turkish-Cypriot authorities of those apprehended at Ayios Kassianos.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the number of demonstrators at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia fluctuated between 200 and 2,000, and that they blocked all UN traffic through this entrance until 30 July 1989, when the Turkish-Cypriot authorities released the last two detainees.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the events created considerable tension in the island and that intensive efforts were made, both at the UN headquarters and at Nicosia, to contain and resolve the situation.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that on 21 July 1989, he expressed his concern at the events and stressed that it was vital that all parties keep in mind the purpose of the UN buffer zone as well as their responsibility to ensure that that area was not violated.
In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that he urged the Turkish-Cypriot authorities to release without delay all those who had been detained.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that on 24 July 1989, the President of the Security Council announced that he had conveyed to the representatives of all the parties, on behalf of the members of the Council, the Council's deep concern at the tense situation created by the incidents of 19 July 1989.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the President of the Security Council stressed the need strictly to respect the UN buffer zone and appealed for the immediate release of all persons still detained, and asked all concerned to show maximum restraint and to take urgent steps to bring about a relaxation of tension and contribute to the creation of an atmosphere favourable to the negotiations.
The applicant produced 21 photographs taken at different times during the demonstration on 19 July 1989.
Photographs 1 to 7 produced by the applicant were intended to show that, notwithstanding the deployment of the Turkish-Cypriot police, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
In photographs 8 to 10 produced by the applicant, members of the Turkish-Cypriot police are seen breaking up the UNFICYP cordon during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The final set of photographs produced by the applicant show members of the Turkish-Cypriot police using force to arrest some of the women demonstrators during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.

The English translation of the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 9 other men, was charged with entering "TRNC" territory without permission, contrary to sections 2, 8 and 9 of Law no. 5/72.

The English translation of the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 9 other men, was charged with entering "TRNC" territory other than through an approved port, contrary to subsections 12(1) and (5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law.
The "TRNC" Nicosia District Court's judgment of 22 July 1989 was given in the presence of the accused and of an interpreter.
The "TRNC" Nicosia District Court noted that the accused did not accept the charges against them and stated that they did not wish to use the services of a lawyer registered in the "TRNC".
The "TRNC" Nicosia District Court noted that the public prosecutor called five witnesses, whose statements were translated into Greek for the accused's benefit.

The "TRNC" Nicosia District Court noted that the witnesses (mainly police officers on duty at the time of the demonstration) declared that the accused had illegally entered the "TRNC" territory, shouted abuse at the Turkish-Cypriot forces and resisted arrest by pulling and pushing.
The "TRNC" Nicosia District Court noted that knives and other cutting objects had been found in the bags of some of the demonstrators who had been arrested.

The "TRNC" Nicosia District Court noted that the applicant stated that he was a journalist, that he had been arrested while he was following the demonstration even though the peacekeeping forces had given him permission to do so.

The "TRNC" Nicosia District Court noted that the accused had been told that they could cross-examine witnesses in turn and, if they so wished, choose one of their number to cross-examine the witnesses on behalf of all the accused, but that they had not done so; one of the accused had put a few questions to one of the prosecution witnesses.

Before the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court passed sentence, the Bishop of Kitium, speaking on behalf of all the accused, made a statement saying that their struggle was peaceful, that their aim was to encourage Greek and Turkish-Cypriots to live together in peace, that they carried no weapons and that they had asked for UN protection.

The "TRNC" Nicosia District Court, relying on statements by the prosecution witnesses which had not been undermined by the statements made by some of the accused, concluded that the accused had crossed the borders of the "TRNC" at an unapproved entry point and without permission and had resisted by various means the UN and Turkish forces which had tried to stop them.
The "TRNC" Nicosia District Court found that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the accused were guilty on both counts.

In deciding on the sentence, the "TRNC" Nicosia District Court took into account the seriousness of the offence and the fact that the accused had shown no remorse and continued to deny the validity of the "TRNC".

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code defines an unlawful assembly as five or more persons assembled with intent to commit an offence, or, being assembled with intent to carry out some common purpose, conducting themselves in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear that the persons so assembled will commit a breach of the peace, or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to commit a breach of the peace.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that it is immaterial that the original assembling was lawful if, being assembled, the persons conduct themselves with a common purpose in such a manner as to cause fear of a breach of the peace.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that when an unlawful assembly has begun to execute the purpose for which it assembled by a breach of the peace and to the terror of the public, the assembly is called a riot and the persons assembled are said to be riotously assembled.
According to section 71 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, any person who takes part in an unlawful assembly is guilty of a misdemeanour and liable to imprisonment for one year.

Section 80 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that any person who carries in public without lawful occasion any offensive arm or weapon in such a manner as to cause terror to any person is guilty of a misdemeanour, liable to imprisonment for two years, and his arm or weapons shall be forfeited.
According to section 82 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, it is an offence to carry a knife outside the home.

Chapter 155, section 14(1)(b) of the Cypriot Criminal Procedure Law states that any police officer may, without warrant, arrest any person who commits in his presence any offence punishable with imprisonment.

Chapter 155, section 14(1)(c) of the Cypriot Criminal Procedure Law states that any police officer may, without warrant, arrest any person who obstructs a police officer while in the execution of his duty.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorization, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act, and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and fine.

On 22 July 1989, there was an angry crowd in the court area shouting, swearing and making obscene gestures at the applicant and the other detainees.
The applicant was detained in Ortakeuy Prison from 24 until 28 July 1989.

During his detention in Ortakeuy Prison from 24 until 28 July 1989, the applicant refused to eat anything in order to protest against the prison director's refusal to give to the Bishop of Kitium the church vestments and holy vessels, which had been sent in order to allow the Bishop to celebrate mass.
On 26 July 1989, the applicant was locked in an isolation cell at Ortakeuy Prison as punishment for refusing food.
The isolation cell at Ortakeuy Prison in which the applicant was placed on 26 July 1989 was extremely small and unbearably hot (40-60°C).

The applicant alleged that his health problems (osteoarthritis of the cervical cord, cervical disc disease, and related conditions) were the result of the savage blows he had received from Turkish policemen, soldiers and civilians in July 1989.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators, supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration, were demanding that the "Green Line" in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.

In his report of 7 December 1989 on the UN operations in Cyprus, the UN Secretary General stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.
In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by UNFICYP and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that in the afternoon of 21 July 1989, some 300 Greek Cypriots gathered at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia to protest the continuing detention by the Turkish-Cypriot authorities of those apprehended at Ayios Kassianos.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the number of demonstrators at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia fluctuated between 200 and 2,000, and that they blocked all UN traffic through this entrance until 30 July 1989, when the Turkish-Cypriot authorities released the last two detainees.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the events created considerable tension in the island and that intensive efforts were made, both at the UN headquarters and at Nicosia, to contain and resolve the situation.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that on 21 July 1989, he expressed his concern at the events and stressed that it was vital that all parties keep in mind the purpose of the UN buffer zone as well as their responsibility to ensure that that area was not violated.
In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that he urged the Turkish-Cypriot authorities to release without delay all those who had been detained.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that on 24 July 1989, the President of the Security Council announced that he had conveyed to the representatives of all the parties, on behalf of the members of the Council, the Council's deep concern at the tense situation created by the incidents of 19 July 1989.

In his report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General stated that the President of the Security Council stressed the need strictly to respect the UN buffer zone and appealed for the immediate release of all persons still detained, and asked all concerned to show maximum restraint and to take urgent steps to bring about a relaxation of tension and contribute to the creation of an atmosphere favourable to the negotiations.
During the demonstration of 19 July 1989, Turkish forces started to beat some women demonstrators with batons, to kick them and drag them by the arms, legs and hair.
While the applicant was trying to help some of the women demonstrators, he was grabbed and beaten by Turkish policemen.
The applicant was hit in the face and other parts of the body by Turkish policemen during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant was taken at gunpoint together with others who had also been arrested during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant's photographic equipment was seized despite him showing his press card during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The applicant was led to a bus through an angry crowd of 200-300 civilians who shouted abuse and threats at him.
As the applicant was walking without police protection, the crowd had an opportunity to rush at him, and he was dragged and beaten until two policemen came and accompanied him onto the bus.
The applicant was transported to the so-called "Pavlides Garage", where a body search was carried out and all his personal effects were taken.
Sometime around midnight at the so-called "Pavlides Garage", the applicant was interrogated by an officer who spoke perfect Greek.
The applicant did not give wholly accurate answers to some of the questions during the interrogation, preferring to lie about some of the detail.
The interrogating officer started a political discussion and tried to convey his own ideas to the applicant in a very friendly and diplomatic manner.
The applicant refused to sign a statement written in Turkish, as he considered it would have been tantamount to recognising the "Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus" (the "TRNC").
When one of the women detainees (Mrs Vrahimi, application no. 16078/90) was beaten at the so-called "Pavlides Garage", all the other prisoners remained silent, fearing for their fate.
At around 2.30 a.m. on 20 July 1989, the applicant and some other men were ordered onto a police bus.
The applicant was taken to the Seray Police Station, where, after a body search, he was held in a cell that was filthy, dirty and dark.
During his stay in the cell at the Seray Police Station, the applicant heard the screams of other demonstrators.
At around 2.00 p.m. on 20 July 1989, the applicant was given back his personal effects and taken to court together with seven other prisoners.
No proper translation was provided at the court hearing on 20 July 1989.
At the court hearing on 20 July 1989, a policeman acted as translator but translated only part of what the judge and the witnesses said.
At the court hearing on 20 July 1989, the accused explained why they were taking part in the demonstration and in what capacity.
The applicant was remanded in custody for two days following the court hearing on 20 July 1989.
The applicant was taken to Ortakeuy Prison, where all his personal effects were removed again.
At Ortakeuy Prison, the applicant was put with other men in a dormitory block.
An hour after being placed in the dormitory block at Ortakeuy Prison, the applicant was blindfolded and led to another area of the prison.
At Ortakeuy Prison, the applicant was interrogated by four or five army officers who could not speak any Greek, with a translator present.
The interrogation at Ortakeuy Prison touched on political and military subjects.
On 21 July 1989, the applicant was again taken to court together with nine other people.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the applicant had no legal representation.

At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, no proper interpretation was provided, and the interpreter had difficulties in translating some of the words and was occasionally helped by the television anchorman.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, one of the accused (the Bishop of Kitium) spoke on behalf of the others and said they would only accept as defence counsel a Greek-Cypriot or a UN lawyer.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the trial judge replied that she could only appoint a lawyer registered with the "TRNC" bar association.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the accused pleaded "not guilty" and stated that they did not recognise the legitimacy of the "TRNC" and of its tribunals.
At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, four witnesses were called by the prosecution.

At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the Bishop of Kitium put some questions to the first prosecution witness, but those considered of a political character were ruled inadmissible by the trial judge.

At the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the Bishop of Kitium made the following statement: "since cross-examining the pseudo-witnesses of your pseudo-court may be regarded as indicating that we recognise the procedure, we say that we have nothing else to say and we shall not cross-examine any other pseudo-witness".
From the point of the Bishop of Kitium's statement at the court hearing on 21 July 1989, the accused did not participate in the procedure.
After the trial hearing on 21 July 1989, the applicant and his co-accused were taken back to prison and their pictures were taken.
On 22 July 1989, the applicant was taken to court again.
On 22 July 1989, a baying crowd gathered outside the courtroom.

On 22 July 1989, there was an angry crowd in the court area shouting, swearing and making obscene gestures at the applicant and the other detainees.
